title: Acoustics: play softly, bass overtones and noise is not music
summary: A California A&R man taught him to record softly; Thomas explains overtones and criticizes loud rock and disco.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: And I got involved with an A&R man in California, and he recorded the Symphony. And I learned so much from him, because he's the one who taught me if you record something soft, you can play it, and you don't have no distortions in it, and you can turn it up loud and it's beautiful.
That's right.
Thomas - 173

And he had the hardest time recording the guitar player. There was a guitar player on it that played the stuff loud, and he kept telling him, "Play it softer." And he explained it to me. He said, "If he plays it soft and I can get it soft, then I can bring it louder. I don't need nothin'."

And you know, I... In my early years, I studied acoustics. And acoustics is a science. I'm going to write out a theory on that, too. You know, overtones go in fifths. Like, you hear the low C, the first fifth is G, the next fifth is D... I've got to memorize so I can tell them right... And the next after D...
Well, why is the next fifth D? If the first one is C to G, why would the next one be D? G, D... I see.
And G to D, and then from D...
How would you do that?
A. I think it was (?) D...
Yeah, it would be G again.
No, wait a minute...
D to A.

Yeah D to A. And see, if the bass is loud enough, them overtones keep going up, and then they finally go up into discord. That's why you get the dissonance. Them discords come in. And that's why the bass should never
Thomas - 174

play too loud. See, because the bass is the beginning of the overtones. And if I play it acoustically... I've heard there's a stop in one of the organs over in England or somewhere, there's one stop in there they can't play because it's like they'll almost draw the building down or something -- some kind of thing like that.

And this guy explained to me about acoustics, why a guy should play soft to start out. If he plays soft, he don't get them overtones in there. He don't get the overtones in there far enough to get the distance. But when...you can turn it up, and it's... What's the word for it? The (?) is full...
We don't want to get too technical.

But that's why I was trying to get him to play softer. Because Bill just puts that darn pedal all the way down to the floor. And that's one thing that's been wrong with so many of the Jazz musicians and the Rock-and-Roll musicians. They play too much noise. And noise ain't music. It ain't gonna never be music. They don't even try. And they've got these electronics that push it up, and the louder you make it, the more overtones you got.
It can just tear your eardrums off.
You know, a lot of the... Years ago... I don't get them (?) any more. But years ago, a lot of the
Thomas - 175

young guys that were in A&R, they'd only know that a record was popular. They got a... I don't understand it. They got a thing that can put...what they call that...? They don't call it Disco? It can put that noise in there. And that don't make sense! That noise ain't what makes the music. It's the beat or either the lyrics or either the melody that makes the song popular.
